title: Information on surgical treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia on YouTube is highly biased and misleading
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of 159 English-language YouTube videos on surgical treatment of LUTS/BPH (search May 2019; up to the 20 most-viewed videos for each of 15 search categories, minimum 500 views). Every video was graded for 'degree of misinformation compared to currently available evidence on surgical BPH treatment as reported by the EAU guidelines' on a five-level scale (no / very little / moderate / high / extreme) by two of six urologist raters independently, with a third arbitrating. The paper reports verbatim shares of items by falsity grade: 21 videos (13.2 %) contained NO misinformation, i.e. 86.8 % provided misinformation (stated verbatim in the Discussion), and 9 videos (5.7 %) provided extreme misinformation. Item-level falsity against an external ground truth (EAU guidelines) with a stated denominator = CONTENT. The parallel DISCERN scores are reported only as medians and produce no share.

estimates.source_quote: For all treatment modalities assessed there were videos showing at least moderate misinformation based on current evidence of surgical BPH treatment 7. In total, only 21 videos (13.2%) were rated to contain no misinformation while nine videos (5.7%) were rated to provide extreme misinformation (Fig. 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results (paragraph 3) and Discussion (paragraph 1: 'provides misinformation compared to the current body of evidence (86.8%)'); Figure 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Six author-raters (three board-certified urologists, Fellows of the European Board of Urology, and three senior residents) each assessed 53 videos; every video was independently rated by two of the six, and any non-identical result on the misinformation grade was arbitrated by a third author (DA, PB). The benchmark was the EAU 'Management of Non-neurogenic Male LUTS' guideline. No kappa or other reliability coefficient is reported; the authors state 'discrepancies were rare' and acknowledge the misinformation grading is a subjective, self-designed scale.
estimates.moderator_quote: An independent video search for surgical treatment options of LUTS/BPH was performed in May 2019 on YouTube by six of the authors. ... All videos included had to have an English audio track and a minimum of 500 views. Instructional surgical videos were excluded from the analysis. For each treatment option, a maximum of 20 videos were subjected to further analysis. If more videos met the inclusion criteria, the 20 videos with the most views were selected.
estimates.notes: 86.8 % is stated VERBATIM in the Discussion, so it is not a complement I computed (R8 satisfied); it also matches 159 - 21 = 138/159 = 86.8 %. CRITICAL THRESHOLD NOTE for an adjudicator: this is the most lenient possible misinformation numerator - any video whose grade was above 'no misinformation', including 'very little', counts. The authors' own five-level scale is self-designed and explicitly described as subjective. The high value should be read alongside the 5.7 % extreme-misinformation row (next row), which uses the strictest grade on the same corpus. Rank-truncated sample (up to the 20 most-viewed per search category, >=500 views), so denom_selection=curated and results are not weighted for views (a stated limitation).

estimates.moderator_quote: Some parts of the video analyses (e.g. rating the extent of misinformation) represent subjective assessments and the rating options were self-designed (e.g. very little, moderate, high, extreme misinformation). We aimed to minimize the potential bias of subjective assessment by independent evaluation of all videos by two authors respectively.
estimates.notes: definition_variant=true: this is the STRICTEST definition of the same construct on the same 159-video corpus as the 86.8 % row (severity grade 'extreme' only). The two rows bracket the measurement: 5.7 % under the strictest reading, 86.8 % under the most lenient. The intermediate grades (very little / moderate / high) are shown only in Figure 1 and are not given numerically in the text, so the middle of the distribution cannot be recovered.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) INTERMEDIATE GRADES NOT RECOVERABLE: the counts for 'very little', 'moderate' and 'high' misinformation appear only in Figure 1 (a stacked colour chart by treatment topic), which the text extraction does not render, so no row for e.g. 'moderate or worse' could be built without summing categories (barred by R8). The statement 'For all treatment modalities assessed there were videos showing at least moderate misinformation' gives no numerator. (2) COMMERCIAL BIAS NOT EXTRACTED AS MISINFORMATION: 26 videos (16.4 %) were free of commercial bias, i.e. 83.6 % were subject to commercial bias (stated verbatim in the Discussion). Commercial bias is a promotional-framing judgement, not a truth/falsity judgement against a ground truth, so it does not meet the CONTENT bar and would at best be QUALITY; I did not create a row, since the review's construct is misinformation prevalence. An adjudicator who wanted a broad 'problematic content' measure would find 83.6 % here. (3) CONFLICT-OF-INTEREST DISCLOSURE (2 videos, 1.3 %) and mention of alternative treatments (71 videos, 44.7 %) are transparency/completeness measures, not falsity. (4) DISCERN: reported as medians per item and per treatment category (overall quality median 2/5; four of 15 categories reached median 3) with no share of videos above any threshold, so no QUALITY row is possible. (5) TREATMENT-CATEGORY SUBGROUPS: Figure 1 breaks misinformation down by each of the 15 treatment categories, but no category-level percentages are given in the text; these would be within-study subgroups in any case. (6) The 63 %-85 % 'irrelevant/poor/very poor' figures in the Discussion are cited from other papers (refs 14, 15) and are excluded by R8. (7) No country is reported for videos or viewers; only English-audio videos on a single platform were included (stated limitations).

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Frame: searches in May 2019 for 14 named surgical BPH treatments plus one 'patient-based' general-term category (keywords in Supplementary Table 1); over 2,000 videos found, 159 included (English audio track, >=500 views, instructional surgical videos excluded), with a cap of the 20 most-viewed per category. Coding: each video randomly assigned to two of six author-raters (three EBU-certified urologists, three senior residents), each rating 53 videos independently; disagreement on the misinformation grade, provider type, primary topic, commercial bias or COI reporting was arbitrated by a third author (DA, PB). Misinformation graded on a self-designed five-level scale against EAU guideline evidence; quality assessed with the validated 16-item DISCERN. Not reported: any inter-rater reliability statistic (the authors say discrepancies were 'rare'), and results are unweighted for views. Stated limitations: English-only, single platform, max 20 videos per topic, subjective self-designed misinformation scale, mixed search results. No commercial incentive declared.
